title: SRE Standards: SLOs, Error Budgets, Capacity Planning, Reliability Initiatives, Incident Review & Runbooks
author: Ari Chen
content:
Overview:

This document codifies Redwood Inference's SRE standards for setting and operating to service-level objectives (SLOs) and error budgets, capacity planning, reliability initiatives, incident review standards, operational tooling, and runbook structure. It is intended to be the canonical reference for teams that operate production services (hosted API, dedicated inference, private deployments).

Goals:
- Ensure clear, measurable SLOs for customer-facing behavior and internal platform health.
- Define a consistent error budget policy and automated guardrails to support safe releases and rollouts.
- Provide a reproducible capacity planning cadence and runbook-driven response for capacity incidents.
- Standardize incident review and postmortem practices to drive reliable remediation and prioritized reliability initiatives.
- Establish minimal operational tooling and runbook templates so on-call engineers can act quickly and predictably.

1) SLOs and Error Budgets

Introduction:
SLOs quantify user-visible reliability and form the primary inputs for error budgets and risk-based decision making (deployments, canaries, rollbacks). Every production service must publish at least one customer-facing SLO and one internal availability/latency SLO.

SLO Format (required):
- Name: short identifier (e.g., "public-api_success_rate_v1").
- Objective: target percentage or percentile (e.g., 99.9% success rate; p95 latency < 300ms).
- Time window: rolling 30d (default) and rolling 7d for short-term monitoring.
- Measurement: Prometheus query or equivalent (provide exact query in the service SLO page).
- Owner: team/service owner contact.

SLO Example (public API):
- Objective: 99.9% successful responses (2xx) per 30d
- Measurement query (PromQL): rate(http_requests_total{job="public-api",code=~"2.."}[30d]) / rate(http_requests_total{job="public-api"}[30d])
- Alerting: trigger when 30d burn > 25% or 7d burn > 50%

Error budget policy:
- Error budget = 1 - SLO. For 99.9% SLO, monthly error budget = 0.1% of user interactions.
- Burn rate thresholds and automated actions:
  1) Normal (0-25% burn): proceed with normal deploy cadence.
  2) Elevated (25-50% burn): no risky releases (no infra changes, database migrations without rollback plan). Team notifies product and SRE.
  3) Constrained (50-100% burn): freeze non-critical releases; roll back recent risky changes; initiate targeted mitigation runbook.
  4) Exhausted (>100% burn): urgent remediation, incident declared if user impact persists; triage meeting within 2 hours.

SLO ownership & reviews:
- Service owners review SLOs quarterly. SRE schedules an annual SLO audit for cross-service consistency.
- When changing SLOs, teams must document impact analysis (customer impact, error budget consequences) and get SRE sign-off for changes that relax objectives.

2) Capacity Planning

Cadence and scope:
- Quarterly capacity review per service + monthly light-check for critical services (public API, routing, KV cache).
- Inputs: traffic growth (QPS, token/sec), request size distribution, model sequence length distribution, regional growth, scheduled campaigns (sales, marketing) and new features.

Capacity planning template (deliverable):
- Current baseline: provisioned GPUs, average and peak utilization (7d, 30d), throttles and queue sizes.
- Forecast: 12-month forecast with 3 scenarios (baseline, +25%, +100%).
- Risk register: single points of failure (zone limits, image build windows), mitigations, required procurement lead times.
- Action plan: capacity add steps, autoscaling config updates, pre-warming schedules, canary rollout windows, and rollback triggers.

Capacity runbook excerpt (on overload):
1) Verify dashboards: confirm increased queue length, GPU utilization > 85% sustained for > 5m, increased latency p95 > baseline by > 2x.
2) Throttle/Reject: activate automated traffic shaping policy for non-priority routes.
3) Scale: trigger autoscaler to add nodes or route traffic to less-loaded regions.
4) Deprioritize: temporarily reduce batch sizes for best-effort jobs and move background jobs to maintenance window.
5) Communicate: page owners, publish update to #sre-ops channel and include ETA and mitigation steps.

3) Reliability Initiatives (RIs)

Definition and prioritization:
- RIs are multi-week projects aimed at improving reliability metrics (SLO attainment, MTTR, capacity headroom).
- Each RI must have: measurable objective (metric & target), owner, scope, success criteria, and 8-week plan with milestones.

RI examples:
- Improve API p95 latency from 350ms -> 220ms under p95 load (investigate kernel scheduling & batching improvements).
- Reduce cold-start latency for private deployments by 40% via pre-warming and snapshotting.

Prioritization rubric:
- Customer impact (SLO burn reduction potential) 40%
- Implementation effort 30%
- Operational risk reduction 20%
- Cross-team dependency complexity 10%

4) Incident Review and Postmortems

Incident declaration and levels:
- Severity 1 (S1): production outage impacting many customers or major data loss. Page within 15 minutes.
- Severity 2 (S2): degraded service with partial customer impact. Page within 60 minutes.
- Severity 3 (S3): minor user impact or internal-only issues. Page as needed.

Postmortem standards (required for S1 and S2 with customer impact):
- Template fields: incident timeline, impact summary, root cause analysis, contributing factors, mitigations applied, action items (owner + due date), follow-up reliability initiative if needed.
- No-blame culture: focus on systemic fixes and process improvements.
- Time-to-postmortem: draft within 3 business days, final within 10 business days.
- Review: postmortems are reviewed in the monthly Reliability Council (SRE + product + engineering leads).

Incident review checklist:
1) Confirm data and metrics used in timeline (logs, traces, dashboards).
2) Reproduce failure mode (if safe and possible) in staging.
3) Validate root cause with at least two independent signals (e.g., logs + trace + infra event).
4) Create concrete action items and assign owners.
5) Track action items in reliability board; require completion before SLO relaxation or similar policy changes.

5) Operational Tooling Minimums

Required tooling for all production services:
- Metrics: Prometheus + Thanos for long-term metrics.
- Dashboards: Grafana with per-service SLO dashboards (30d and 7d windows) and an SRE org-level reliability board.
- Tracing: Jaeger/OpenTelemetry for distributed traces with automatic sampling config per service.
- Logging: centralized ELK stack or hosted alternative with 90d retention for customer-facing services.
- Alerting: PagerDuty integrated with playbooks; alerts must map to specific runbooks and include runbook links in messages.
- CI/CD: pipeline must support canaries, automated rollback, and deployment annotations that surface in the SLO dashboard.

Operational automation examples:
- Automated SLO burn alerts (PromQL + Grafana alerting) that trigger both Slack and PagerDuty based on threshold tiers.
- Canary analysis automation: for canary rollouts, run automated A/B comparison for latency and error rates; if burn delta > threshold, abort.

6) Runbooks and Playbooks

Runbook structure (required header fields):
- Service, runbook name, owner, severity scope, pre-conditions, quick checklist, full remediation steps, verification steps, rollback steps, post-incident actions, contact list.

Runbook checklist (public API high-latency example):
1) Check SLO dashboard link (30d and 7d).
2) Identify affected routes and models via request logs / trace tags.
3) If GPU saturation: reduce batch size -> verify latency.
4) If upstream dependency failing: switch traffic to fallback model variant.
5) If recent deploy in last 60 minutes: roll back to previous tagged release.
6) Notify customers with affected SLAs via status page.

Runbook best practices:
- Keep runbooks short (< 1 screen for quick triage) with a single-line TL;DR at the top.
- Keep verification queries and exact CLI/PromQL snippets in the runbook.
- Maintain runbook ownership and quarterly tests (game days) to ensure runbook accuracy.

7) Ownership, Training & Game Days

- Ownership: each service must declare SLO owner and on-call rotation in the service README. SRE will assist in SLO setup and runbook reviews.
- Training: mandatory on-call bootcamp for new on-call engineers covering this document, alert triage, and runbook usage.
- Game days: quarterly simulated incidents for high-risk services; results feed into reliability initiatives and runbook updates.

8) Change Control and Exceptions

- Any exception to SLO policy, error budget actions, or runbook minimums must be recorded in the risk-and-exceptions tracker and approved by SRE + service manager.
- Temporary relaxations for major product launches require a documented rollback plan and an explicit error budget acceptance threshold.

Appendices

A. Example PromQL snippets:
- Success rate (30d): sum(rate(http_requests_total{job="public-api",code=~"2.."}[30d])) / sum(rate(http_requests_total{job="public-api"}[30d]))
- P95 latency (7d): histogram_quantile(0.95, sum(rate(http_request_duration_seconds_bucket{job="public-api"}[7d])) by (le))

B. Runbook template (one-line TL;DR then steps) — available as a downloadable .md on the service page.

C. Contacts and channels:
- #sre-ops (primary), #platform-build (secondary), pagerduty: Redwood SRE on-call.

Document ownership and updates:

- Review cadence: quarterly.
